source.title: Extreme Memorization via Scale of Initialization
source.authors: Harsh Mehta; Ashok Cutkosky; Behnam Neyshabur

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices; no relevant cut-off is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies initialization scale and finds that overparameterized networks can fit natural training labels while test performance falls toward chance; results also vary with activation, loss, dataset, and training setup. This qualifies the general claim that standard training on natural data yields low test error.
record.gate_note: Reports results on natural-label image datasets and shuffled-label representation alignment. The shuffled-label result is stated as an expectation and figure description, not as a measured train/test accuracy result. Alignment values are measurements tied to generalization, but exact numerical values are figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study tests V3 through its own CIFAR-10 architecture comparison: adding convolution and pooling improves test accuracy over a fully connected MLP, with further improvements for ResNet-50 and DenseNet-121. Initialization-scale experiments do not establish V1's paired random-label fitting and natural-label generalization result.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. Increasing initialization scale degrades generalization, most extremely with sin activation; ReLU effects are attributed to the loss function, and sigmoid scaling can also impair training. Alignment correlates empirically with generalization across several settings, although the conclusion identifies extremely low initialization scales as a possible exception.
record.recipe_differences: Studies initialization scale and alignment in overparameterized networks rather than reproducing the listed original studies. Uses two-layer MLPs, varied activations and losses, and a separate architecture comparison; SGD without momentum, fixed learning rate and batch size, and no explicit regularizers in the main experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization scale; activation function; loss function; dataset; architecture; for sin activation, first-layer learning rate and whether first-layer weights are frozen. Squared-loss scaling is constrained by divergence at larger scales; sigmoid gradients vanish beyond a scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing initialization scale degrades natural-label test performance, reaching chance performance with perfect training fit for sin networks; effects depend on activation and loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization scale controls generalization in the tested SGD-trained image classifiers, with activation- and loss-dependent effects.

fits_no_version.finding: In-class gradient and representation alignment correlate with generalization across initialization scales and architectures; shuffled labels reduce representation alignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-class alignment correlates with generalization in these experiments, with an exception suggested at extremely low initialization scales.

fits_no_version.finding: High-scale memorization persists across a range of first-layer learning rates; freezing that layer leaves imperfect training fit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The high-scale memorization phenomenon is robust to some first-layer learning-rate changes, while frozen features and excessive learning rates impair training fit.

record.problems: Most relevant numerical results are shown only in plots, without transcribed values or uncertainty estimates. The principal initialization experiments use one large hidden layer and a fixed SGD recipe; the architecture comparison also fixes hyperparameters across architectures. Shuffled-label accuracy is not reported in the supplied text as a numerical result.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out; all separately described dataset, activation/loss, architecture, and learning-rate findings captured within the 60-row limit. Several figure-only plots include multiple training metrics, but only the principal test/generalization measure and stated distinctions are recorded.

untested.parts: A matched demonstration of near-perfect fixed-random-label fitting, above-chance natural-label test accuracy, and chance random-label test accuracy under the same architecture and training recipe.
Width sweeps beyond the zero-training-error threshold and their test-error trends.

The contribution of local connectivity separately from pooling, weight sharing, depth and capacity; learned sparse local connections; initialization from a trained convolutional network; datasets other than CIFAR-10.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning budgets, weight-decay variants and optimizer switching.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout comparisons, training-set-size dependence and removal of dropout with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus equally sized random removals followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V3. Its initialization results do not challenge V1's specific coexistence claim. No numerical plot values can be recovered from the supplied text. The record's assertion that all findings were captured overlooks four-layer experiments and the low-scale learning-rate sweep, but these omissions do not bear on the listed versions.

versions.untested_parts: Tests initialization-scale effects on natural-label datasets, not the same architectures and training recipes on both fixed random and natural labels with reported train and test accuracy.
No width sweep past the zero-training-error threshold.
Does not test learned sparse local connections or a fully connected network initialized from a trained convolutional network.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD.
Measures gradient and representation alignment, not magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Does not remove memorized examples and retrain.
